Troy Deeney has given his Newcastle United verdict.

The BBC Sport pundit talking after the weekend’s match at Craven Cottage.

This comes as Troy Deeney picks his best 12 performers from the top tier action.

The Premier League team of the weekend (and manager) that have most impressed him.

Included in his dozen choices is somebody who was the standout ‘unbelievable’ performer on Saturday afternoon in West London.

Newcastle United drawing 1-1 away against Fulham.

Troy Deeney explains why he has chosen this player from the match at Craven Cottage for his Premier League team of the week and then the full eleven (twelve) are listed below:

“Bernd Leno (Fulham): Unbelievable couple of saves from him to keep Fulham in the game. I thought Newcastle should have been three or four up before Fulham got the equaliser.”

Lukas Hornicek made some smart saves but United had comfortably more clear chances and could/should have won the game if not for the excellence of Bernd Leno. Though even he could do nothing about Jacob Murphy’s stunner.

Troy Deeney Premier League team of the week:

Bernd Leno (Fulham) Ronald Araujo (Liverpool) Jair Cunha (Nottingham Forest) Tarik Muharemovic (Leeds United) Nordi Mukiele (Sunderland) Leon Goretzka (Aston Villa) Alexis Mac Allister (Liverpool) Enzo Le Fee (Sunderland) Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall (Everton) Thierno Barry (Everton) Liam Delap (Nottingham Forest)

#2090. First Newcastle United match of the Premier League season but hopefully not the last

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The first live Premier League Newcastle United match of the season for us.

Albeit sat in the supposed home supporters end at Craven Cottage.

I wake up early to a London pea souper. By midday the mist is starting to lift and we are on the train to Putney.

It is then a walk across Putney Bridge to Archbishop’s Park. It is on this walk over the bridge where we see our first half and half scarf. Oh dear.

After a few beers with our Fulham friends it is off to Craven Cottage which is wedged between the river and streets of beautiful Victorian housing. A classic example of a football club from a different era and hemmed in from that time.

Through the turnstiles at the rear of the Cottage and then we are in our seats in row ZZ, the back row to be precise.

I have been in the Putney end many times but on this occasion there appears to be fewer black and white stripes on show than previously. But significantly there is a lot of half and half scarves. An awful creation which has a crest with the words Geordie Boys inside it.

We stand during the minute’s silence for Remembrance Day and a young man and his partner take their seats in the row in front of us talking loudly, mobile phones in hands. A woman turns around and tells them to “shut up and show some respect.”

We start the game brightly but it turns into another game like Palace. The highlight is the Dan Burn goal which we celebrate but are completely baffled at it being disallowed as we have probably got the worst seats in the house to make any reasoned judgement.

Twenty minutes into the game and groups of people start leaving their seats, some wearing half and halfs. This cycle goes on throughout the game, small groups moving in and out. Other spectators stand up and start recording with their phones, or taking selfies, blocking our line of sight as the game is happening.

At this moment I realise now why my Chelsea mates are so vexed, as this is what they have described to me, but even worse for them as it is happening in their main end, the Matthew Harding stand.

No wonder they are angry. I was getting angry and we were in the Fulham end.

Second half we start brightly and I am hopeful for another Palace-like after the break performance.

Before the game my son had said “I am going home if Jacob Murphy starts”, so down on the winger he is.

A big Geordie lad has spotted us and the adjacent tourist seat that has been vacated, he joins us. We have the perfect view of the Murphy goal and we celebrate like we were in the Gallowgate End.

Three minutes later and you are reminded of what it is to be a Newcastle United fan.

The trudge through the park back to Putney station, me and my lad debate how poor the referee was and the reasons for it.

First Newcastle United match of the Premier League season but hopefully not the last.

#2089. The state of the atmosphere at St James’ Park, Selhurst Park and what can be done?

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Reading Greg McPeake’s article on The Mag (‘Interesting what these Chelsea fans had to say in the pub the other week’ – 1 Nov) about Chelsea fans giving up their season tickets because they’ve become too expensive, made me think about recurring comments on The Mag and elsewhere about Newcastle United fans and the changing demographics inside St James’ Park on match day.

One description that I’ve seen seems to sum up both the change and the general effect this may be having – that we now have a stadium full of spectators rather than fans.

This was part of the case argued by Chris Hall in his article (‘An open letter to Newcastle United fans’ – 8 Nov) which examined in detail what he sees as the changed atmosphere generated nowadays at St James Park and the reasons for that.

Reaction to that article was, unsurprisingly polarised, with people either praising it for hitting the nail on the head or slamming it as uninformed “bobbins”!

Chris was either exposing the reality of the “Fortress SJP” myth, or exposing his own lack of real experience in a frantic effort to blame the Newcastle United fans for the club’s failings. Take your pick.

I’m not setting out to insult or denigrate anyone by bringing up this issue. I’m well aware that, despite the continuing emphasis on growing the commercial side of match day, the stadium is still rammed with tens of thousands of passionate Geordies – but as season ticket holders of long standing they are inevitably growing longer in the tooth. The passion is, maybe, now internalised and reserved for the more extreme moments rather than roaring out in youthful exuberance throughout the match.

Thus speaks the man who hasn’t ventured inside St James’ Park since the day that internalised passion was released to roundly boo off Moussa Sissoko during a dire home defeat to Bournemouth! I would also like to point out, though, that any reservations regarding the home supporters as a body do NOT apply to the away fans who often show up the home supporters in their own grounds.

Anyway, my aim here wasn’t to focus so much on our supporters but to raise the issue in a wider context, using the example of another club who we played recently – Crystal Palace.

Being a self-professed expert on the state of places I don’t actually go to, I have for years regarded Selhurst Park as one of the last bastions (at Premier League level) of the “real” game. An old fashioned stadium in the heart of the local community with what seems to be an energetic and noisy working class fan base. It certainly comes over that way on the TV and I always enjoy the passion and volume of the Palace fans.

Despite their recent trophy successes – or maybe I should be saying BECAUSE of those successes – Palace are currently struggling in the Premier League. Midweek European games on top of season after season selling their best players has finally caught up with them, it would seem. Things have become so bad that they even contrived to lose at home …… to us!

When reading the Palace fans’ post-match comments on The Mag. I was struck by two references in particular regarding the atmosphere. One referred to our supporters completely out-singing theirs and offering up the ditty, “shall we sing a song for you?” I must say, it was noticeable on the TV that our guys were consistently louder than theirs – something I don’t normally expect at Selhurst Park. In contrast with Darren Henderson’s assertion, in what I thought was an excellent article, (‘Newcastle United on the road to nowhere via Putney Bridge’) published on The Mag on Bonfire Night, that our away support has become “stagnant”, my ears confirmed that it was very much vibrant and in full flow at Selhurst Park on this occasion at least.

Some other comments set me off on understanding why this was possible. These other comments referred to the absence of the “HF”. Visitors to Selhurst Park will know that the popular end of the ground is the Holmsdale Road end and that Palace have a tradition of their most committed supporters gathering there and being orchestrated by a core group of “ultras” known as the Holmsdale Fanatics.

Ultras are very much a European phenomenon – the hard core of the home support, inevitably dressed primarily in black and using a variety of aids, such as drums, megaphones, pyrotechnics and “choirmasters”, to increase noise levels and lead the support within the stadium. They are not generally associated with British teams. Indeed, new Palace manager Pierre Sage stated that a key reason he decided to take charge of the club is because it was one of the only clubs in the Premier League that had ultras. He didn’t mention salary ….

The group was founded in December 2005 by a small number of supporters who had attended matches together since childhood in the 1980s. They traditionally stood in Block B of the Holmsdale Road Stand since 1999 but have had a bit of a running battle with the club, especially following stadium regulations introduced as a result of the Taylor report, which they described as restrictive. They have since been relocated within that end of the ground in, I believe, Block E.

It is this group that has been responsible for the organised displays and coordinated support that has generated much of the energy and noise that I have always associated with the Selhurst Park home crowd. However, that has sadly now (for Palace fans at least) come to an end.

On 28 Aug 2026, they announced that they were disbanding. The Sun quoted their spokesman as stating:

“Increasingly driven out by the sky high ticket prices, needless restrictions that are designed to strip away the dignity of supporters and relentless harassment and legal action, many young people are choosing to opt out of a game which seems determined to push them away.

“There needs to be a drastic shift at Palace towards younger fans and a move away from a culture in which people attend the ground expecting to be entertained, towards a culture of supporters turning up to play an active role in influencing the result.”

Ticket price rises forcing traditional, working class supporters and youngsters away. Longstanding supporters having to give up season tickets as referenced by Greg’s Chelsea supporting pals. Youngsters being priced out of match day and being replaced by “tourists” prepared to pay the commercial rates for a one-off experience. These are familiar refrains – not just emanating from Monkseaton but increasingly from all other corners of Geordieland. Spectators rather than fans!

The quote continues, elaborating on the issue of mounting displays and using flags and banners during the match:

“From fighting for the most basic of rights just to take materials into Selhurst and stand up in Block B in the early days, to never ending problems with the club right up to the present day, we have been uncompromising in fighting for what we believe in and the rights of football supporters everywhere.”

At St James’ Park, Wor Flags suspended their activities due to Mike Ashley and his lack of support for Rafa Benitez in particular. Fortunately, they were not just welcomed back by the new owners but positively encouraged.

The Holmsdale Fanatics have clearly not enjoyed that kind of relationship with the Palace hierarchy. For whatever reason, I would argue that this has been to the detriment of the club because of the consequent deterioration, now, in the match day atmosphere.

Another key issue that crops up in relation to clubs throughout the country is an inevitable outcome of the aforementioned Taylor Report and that is the fact that, due to the requirement for grounds to be all seater, it is impossible for groups of like-minded supporters to simply gather together within the stadia and choose where they sit/stand (even in home areas of safe standing).

“But the current set up is unsustainable. We have repeatedly warned the club that like-minded fans cannot congregate at Palace in the numbers required to sustain a growing active supporter culture.”

My last visit to SJP, to the ill-fated Bournemouth match mentioned above, required an expedition to the heights of Level 7. Probably the “final frontier” of like-minded congregation, Kind Mike put a stop to it all by relocating the season tickets to other parts of the ground. That despite them serenading him with his own special song! It seems to me as an external observer since then that the atmosphere hasn’t been the same.

The BBC on 28 Aug 2026 carried the Holmesdale spokesman’s reference to the away day experience. It sounds quite bleak but I don’t think it mirrors the experience of our own fans judging by comments I read on The Mag and elsewhere.

“The story away from home is even more dire. In domestic away fixtures, supporters are banned from bringing materials into stadiums, coaches are regularly stopped, and fans are arrested. Away ends across the country are increasingly dominated by older fans, with the next generation failing to come through in significant numbers.”

As I mentioned earlier in the article, our away supporters seem to have a fair proportion of younger lads in their midst – something confrmed for me by my special correspondent, Mr Tony Malabar, who travels away to every game.

The Palace quotes end with a note of pride, however:

“Given these conditions, we have immense pride in all the group has achieved over the past 20 years. From being at the heart of the protests that rescued the club in 2010, to securing the away ticket price cap that has saved working class people millions and supporting the club through a record breaking period, the Holmesdale Fanatics has helped write a chapter in the club’s history that many did not believe was possible.”

They say that they will continue to attend matches but just as a group of mates rather than an organised “ultras” group.

So what? That’s Crystal Palace not us! Or is it?

I freely admit to being an armchair fan. I have never had a season ticket. In my younger days I couldn’t afford it and, anyway, preferred to play sport rather than watch it. Later, I had what I considered more pressing family commitments and moved away to work elsewhere in the country. I now live about 800 hundred miles South West of Newcastle.

My impressions are necessarily gained via Sky/TNT Sports, what my few season ticket-holding mates have to say and conversations on the likes of The Mag. They may well be accurate but could just as easily be wide of the mark. It would therefore be interesting to read your comments in response to the article.

Has the game gone? Have individual seats left aged, ex boot boys too exposed to express themselves? Are the Instagram day trippers taking over? Is the bubble set to burst?

Should we all be singing an altered refrain from the Palace club anthem?

“You say that you love (Say you love me) All of the time (All of the time) You say that you need me (Say you need me) You’ll always be mine (Always be mine) I’m Feeling Sad All Over Baby I’m Sad All Over ….”

#2088. ‘I like him a lot’ – Romelu Lukaku has been mindblown by Liverpool player he could face tonight

Romelu Lukaku has joined the ever-growing fan club of teenage Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha, having been impressed by what he’s seen from the 18-year-old.

The youngster has earned widespread praise for his effervescent performances since breaking into the Reds’ first team last year and has started all three Champions League games so far under Andoni Iraola.

He had to be content with 25 minutes or so off the bench against Arsenal on Sunday and was kept quiet by a sturdy Gunners defence, but his direct running has left an impression on the experienced Belgian striker, who he’ll face tonight in our European clash against Fenerbahce.

Lukaku was speaking to TNT Sports ahead of the fixture at the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium, and he highlighted the threat that Liverpool pose in midfield and attack, with the 33-year-old singling out Ngumoha for praise.

The ex-Manchester United and Everton marksman said: “Offensively they are very good as well. I like Rio. I like him a lot, very direct. I saw his game that he played against Arsenal.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Ngumoha gave arguably his best Liverpool performance in their most recent Champions League outing, the 4-3 win over Villarreal a fortnight ago when he tormented the LaLiga side in completing seven out of the eight dribbles that he attempted (Sofascore).

In many ways he’s almost the antithesis of Lukaku, who’s a towering target man more renowned for power than pace, but the Fenerbahce striker is no less admiring of the teenage winger’s qualities.

The 18-year-old has exuded fearlessness ever since his first-team breakthrough at Anfield, and we highly doubt he’d be overawed by the febrile atmosphere of the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium if he starts tonight.

If Ngumoha can deliver another big performance for Liverpool in Istanbul and the Reds maintain their 100% Champions League record under Iraola, the case for tying him down to a bumper new contract would be strengthened even further.

Lewis Steele has reliably communicated that a new deal should be a matter of when and not if for the teenager, who’s already making a serious impression on his far more experienced peers.

#2086. Michael Carrick answers Man Utd quit question as crisis hits alarming new low

Michael Carrick insisted he would not walk away from Manchester United after Sunday’s wild 4-4 draw with Aston Villa ensured his side would spend the international window languishing in the relegation zone.

Stoppage-time goals from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu saw United rally for an unlikely point on a day when they started both halves by allowing Villa to storm into two-goal leads before coming back.

The point means United sit 18th in the table, doing little to ease the intense scrutiny on Carrick given they are now eight league games without a win – a club record in the Premier League era – with their only victory of the season back in August against newly-promoted Ipswich.

Read more: Haissem Hassan Celtic absence explained as ‘manoeuvring’ costs winger

Asked on Sky Sports if he would quit if he felt it was the right thing to do for the club, Carrick said: “That’s not going to happen.”

Then, speaking in his post-match press conference, Carrick expressed confidence his side could still turn things around this season.

“One hundred per cent,” he said. “I think there’s more than enough. Goals change games and we’ve got to deal with it and it’s something we have to improve on drastically. But there’s more than enough, we’re just making it too difficult for ourselves at the moment in certain times…

“I’m quite clear with what direction the club needs to go in. We’ve just got to win games.”

United were 2-0 down inside five minutes as Alysson and Nicolas Jackson pounced on defensive errors, but Bruno Fernandes got one back from the penalty spot before Youri Tielemans scored against his former club.

Having worked so hard to get level, United conceded twice in the opening seven minutes of the second half to John McGinn’s penalty and Leon Goretzka’s first Villa goal, with many fans having left before their second comeback of the afternoon.

“Football is about moments, football is about what happens in both boxes in the end,” Carrick added.

“Take (away) the moments and the totally avoidable goals we’ve given away, I actually thought we played pretty well, we were the better team for the most part and I’m disappointed we haven’t won the game.”

Unai Emery, among the candidates touted as a potential successor to Carrick, was visibly frustrated at conceding the late equaliser.

“The referee added six minutes, I think the match was done…” Emery said. “I am angry of course. How to accept to lose in the last six minutes with two goals is difficult…

“I’m angry not with the players, angry with the situation. You are winning in the last six minutes, winning in extra time, and we lost the opportunity to have two points more.”

Dorgu headed in from a corner in a crowded penalty box and Emery admitted goalkeeper Zion Suzuki, hugely impressive since joining this summer, still has work to do.

“It is a process, it’s a good example when you concede, it’s (about) adaptation to the Premier League for Zion,” he added.

“They are pushing, they are disturbing the goalkeeper. In some countries, in other leagues, they are not permitting it.

“Here yes, and we have to continue analysing, having experiences and trying to avoid these situations.”

Here at The Mag we invited a number of regular/irregular contributors to give us their Newcastle United heroes and villains.

Our thanks to Dave Marshall for taking up the challenge.

Dave has looked back at his Newcastle United heroes and villains across the various decades when he has been supporting NUFC.

Over to Dave for his Newcastle United heroes and villains down the years.

This brought back a lot of memories – left off dozens of names that were worthy contenders for each of these.

In the end, I had to go with gut over logic sometimes.

Cult Hero: David Kelly: the goals that kept us up in 1992.

Villain: Ruud Gullit: dropped Shearer for the derby – then lost

Lesser Villain: Douglas Hall: 1998 tabloid sting, comments about the fans, setting the tone for how owners treat fans.

2000s Co-Heroes Sir Bobby Robson and Alan Shearer: I cannot choose between them.

Cult hero Obafemi Martins: the somersaults, the pace, the occasional genius.

Lesser villain Dennis Wise: the quiet structural damage.

2010s Hero Rafa Benítez: restored the club’s self-respect.

2020s Hero Amanda Staveley: without her, there’s no Eddie, Bruno, etc. and the cup drought no doubt persists.

Cult hero Allan Saint-Maximin or Jonjo Shelvey.

Villain Alexander Isak: the club have yet to recover.

Lesser villain Dan Ashworth: built it, then left for Manchester United.

#2084. Parker’s past threatens to haunt him over “dire football’ warning | West Ham News

Ask any West Ham fan after last weekend’s 3-1 home loss to West Bromwich Albion whether they’d settle for winning ways at all costs and most would have instantly nodded their agreement.

The second three goal loss at home within eight days had caused the boos to ring out as Nuno’s West Ham train derailed spectacularly, in what was to prove his last game and his ultimate undoing.

Right now there’s a relief flooding around the club as a former hero has returned to take over from negative Nuno. Long may it continue.

However the suggestions are that Parker may not prove to be the all-conquering hero that West Ham seek, judging from his impact at previous clubs. Yes, he knows how to get out of this division and yes, he sure can fix a porous defence – Burnley’s statistics speak for that.

But according to footballleagueworld.co.uk’s article this morning, his time at Burnley divided supporters with his grim, gritty style of play offering little in the way of entertainment:

“The football’s dire. He will bore you to death, and he will cause a fanbase to turn through little snide little comments. He will cause the West Ham fanbase to turn on it.

And that has happened at every single club consistently.”

Few will complain if Scott Parker gets West Ham promoted

Writes their Burnley fan columnist Aaron Wright, condemning Parker’s management style – not results – in the strongest possible terms.

“This is the biggest job he could get, if he can’t get them promoted slash win the league, and if he can’t then keep them in the Premier League, he needs to rethink pretty much everything. He is never getting a bigger job than this and his reputation as a player has helped him get this one. It’s the most guaranteed promotion you will ever have.

“The West Ham fans won’t enjoy it, but I think there’ll be a good respect to it if it turns out how Burnley’s did. 33 games unbeaten is something else.”

Which will have to be a price worth paying, simply to climb back out of this league after the mess of last season and save West Ham from the financial armageddon that not getting promoted would surely deliver.

To paraphrase Jacob Steiberg, Guardian journalist, on Parker’s football shortcomings not succeeding in the Premier League: worry about that next season – first you have to make it back.

From the old Bobby Moore Upper to the Billy Bonds' stand these days - I've been watching since '03 and a supporter since about 1970.. Favourite player - Dean Ashton: Curse you Shaun Wright-Phillips. I still watch YouTube repeats of the Cup Final of 2006 hoping in vain that Shaka Hislop grows another six inches and stops Steven Gerrard's injury time equaliser. Can tell I'm getting old knowing I watched both Mark Noble's debut and his last game at West Ham. Pulling on a Claret and Blue replica shirt still makes me feel the same butterflies as when I was seven years old. Magic.

The Burnley fan sums up my feelings on this by saying this is the biggest club he has managed. You can only work with the tools you are given and he has strong attacking players at West Ham, unlike Nuno, he will quickly learn that we can’t sit on a result and I think that should give us some entertaining games this season.

Like everybody says we’ve heard how his teams can be unadventurous or dull. I do think with these young players in the Championship plus some excellent experienced players, team will always play best on the front foot.

Not 5 at the back, not on the counterattack (not enough pace), not pragmatic (relatively weak defensively) but pressing forwards, quick passes, give and go,.. because we have skillful, quick thinking players. That is what suits them so I hope he will choose this approach which is best adapted to the style of player we have in the squad.

PL a whole different story, where the many young players who might have learnt to handle the Ch. will need to step up yet another level, some experienced players beaten for speed in the PL, etc. That is when I wonder what Parker will do and I hope he can build a team spirit and togetherness with what he has, through this season, the way Leeds & Sunderland did, so as to survive in the PL with some key recruits of course.

Little snide comments I can live with massive Mendes backhanders for the wrong 2 players to keep us up was despicable towards our club, our fans & his hugely paid job (could have easily loaned 2 proven premiership players on a big bonus to keep us up)

I like many have been critical of his previous jobs as being dull and wouldn’t be my choice. But what do I know? He was a great player both technically gifted and a hard worker. Whatever my opinion I will get behind him and back him. #2083. West Ham Exclusive: Gold Share Transfers Now Completed

Sources close to West Ham have revealed to Claret & Hugh that share transactions to complete the transfer of Gold Trust shares have now been completed but are yet to be publicly announced.

Daniel Křetínský used his veto to block the termination of Nuno last summer, when a clause would have allowed the club to pay no compensation for his exit after relegation. As the largest shareholder, he gave his approval to sack Nuno earlier this week, with the compensation package just under £3m.

On 4 September 2026, West Ham released a brief statement confirming that Daniel Křetínský’s 1890s Holdings had reached an agreement to become the club’s single largest shareholder, noting that no further comment would be made until transactions were finalised.

What exactly is holding up the announcement and Daniel Křetínský making a statement on his vision is unclear, with the club mute on the subject.

#2082. Liverpool team news v Fenerbahce: Iraola shuffles the pack with 5 changes, Isak and Wirtz benched

Liverpool put their 100% record in the Champions League on the line this evening as they take on Fenerbahce in Istanbul.

It’s a third visit to the city in just over 13 months for the Reds, having played (and lost to) Galatasaray twice in Turkiye last season, and there’ll be a familiar face in the opposition dugout as Dirk Kuyt takes charge of the home side.

Andoni Iraola welcomed back Dominik Szoboszlai and Victor Munoz from injury in the weekend defeat to Arsenal, but the visitors will be without Ryan Gravenberch as he misses out due to a heel issue.

This is the penultimate assignment of a hectic nine-match fixture sequence for Liverpool in between the two international windows, and the burning question is to what extent the head coach has rotated just three days on from losing to the Gunners.

Iraola has made five changes from the starting XI which lost to Arsenal on Sunday.

Alisson Becker continues in goal behind the familiar centre-back pairing of Jeremy Jacquet and Virgil van Dijk, although both full-backs are changed as Joe Gomez and Kostas Tsimikas come in to start, with Ronald Araujo and Milos Kerkez dropping to the bench.

Trey Nyoni and Alexis Mac Allister keep their places in midfield, and a reshuffle of the attacking unit sees Dominik Szoboszlai, Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz all come into the starting XI. #2081. Veltman’s West Ham Admission Highlights Parker’s First Big Problem

West Ham defender Joël Veltman has admitted that the Hammers’ habit of starting matches poorly must change, with Scott Parker facing an immediate challenge against Blackburn Rovers this afternoon.

Speaking in an interview with the club’s official website, Veltman acknowledged that Wednesday’s disastrous first half against Cardiff City was hardly an isolated incident. West Ham recovered from three goals down to draw 3-3, but the Dutchman knows they cannot keep relying on second-half comebacks.

“It wasn’t the first time we haven’t started so well,” admitted Veltman, who wants West Ham to begin against Blackburn with the same intensity they showed after the interval in Wales.

Personally, I think West Ham’s slow starts and early capitulations are definitely a mentality problem. Nothing demonstrated that more clearly than the transformation at half-time against Cardiff, when a team that had looked completely traumatised and shell-shocked suddenly emerged looking like an entirely different side.

Of course, some of that improvement was tactical, but I’m not entirely convinced how many tactics you can impart in 15 minutes. What Parker, Mark Noble and Jarrod Bowen clearly managed to do was give the players a lift, and the difference in their attitude was extraordinary.

I’ve thought from day one that this was probably the easiest improvement any new manager could make with the current group of players. If West Ham approach matches with a positive attitude and a genuine desire to win rather than playing fearfully, I suspect much of the problem could be addressed with a decent team talk.

That doesn’t mean tactics and team selection are irrelevant, but the players have already demonstrated they possess considerably more ability than their recent performances suggest. Parker’s first job is surely to convince them of that.

Veltman himself was absolutely brilliant during the second half against Cardiff, and I think he could become an important player under Parker. His composure and positioning at right-back could allow Jarrod Bowen the freedom to drift into central areas, where the West Ham captain caused absolute havoc on Wednesday evening.

Bowen was instrumental in the comeback, and having a dependable defender behind him could make that attacking freedom much easier to accommodate. It’s another reason why I’d like to see Veltman retain his place against Blackburn.

The defender certainly recognises the opportunity ahead, telling the club: “We want to go into another away game on Saturday and start where we finished.”

That really is the challenge for Parker. West Ham don’t need to discover some previously hidden ability between now and kick-off; they need to reproduce the confidence, aggression and positive mentality they finally showed during those remarkable 45 minutes against Cardiff.

#2080. Changes forecast for Parker’s first fixture but one puzzle remains | West Ham News

Depending on which outlet you read, West Ham’s newly appointed manager plans two, three or even four changes today as the Hammers take on Blackburn Rovers with the possibility of a rise to third place beckoning depending win other results in this madcap league.

Ezra Mayers and Joel Piroe seem by all accounts to be the most likely duo to benefit from Scott Parker’s new broom. Young Mayers in particular performed creditably considering he’s had no match time since August and Morato’s clumsy performance has surely put him back onto the bench unless a centre-back is needed.

Taty Castellanos’ poor first half was contrasted by Joel Piroe’s instant impact: A pretty unanimous ‘thumbs up’ suggests Piroe will start, after assisting in one of the Irons’s three strikes on Wednesday night. Without looking a world beater, Piroe surely wins the starting place over a moody, ineffective Taty who just continues to disappoint in this league. As football fancast put it:

“Castellanos showed enough potential to create the assumption that he would walk through the Championship. To say that has not happened would be the understatement of the year.”

But the real head-scratcher is why there’s not been more noise around the goal keeper situation after Mads Hermansen let in nine goals in three successive games without laying a glove on any of the attempts.

Mads Hermansen was many people’s choice this season but he hasn’t improved on the fragility shown last year

With the existing ‘connection’ between Scott Parker and Hammers number two Alphonse Areola, most had assumed the new manager would instantly re-instate the ‘keeper who he bought to Fulham and who has been waiting, out of favour, thought this season despite Hermansen’s patchy form. The Dane was even dropped by his international side for a couple of the Nations League ties last month but still, seemingly, could do no wrong under Nuno.

Mystery solved this afternoon, perhaps, when the side is announced. I’m sure most Irons supporters would rather see Areola at the top of the team sheet: No doubt a little rusty but more confidence-inspiring than his counterpart.

#2078. Blackburn Rovers 0 – 0 West Ham United | Half time report

A cold crisp afternoon, perfect for football saw West Ham seemingly doing their best to get into their opponent’s half after the last three weeks’ slow, ponderous starts. The Hammers spent the early moments camped in Blackburn’s half, accompanied by the noise of 7000 visiting fans making Ewood Park sound more like London Stadium on a good day.

Most of West Ham’s early movement was through Mayers and Austbø down the left, the two combining well with the full back pushed right forward in an adventurous set up by Scott Parker.

However it was Blackburn who almost struck first thanks to an overlap down their right and a shot that looped agonisingly over Hermansens’ goal. Mayers responded by fizzing one cross just out of reach of Piroe -nil nil at 20 minutes.

Engels, Austbo and Mayers combined well as the Hammers attacked repeatedly down Blackburn’s left, Austbø impressing in place of Solomon. Half an hour gone and few scares for West Ham:  A more competitive, aggressive start than in recent weeks. Piroe had one ball played through but his lack of pace allowed defenders to crowd him out.

The half continued in the same vein, West Ham looking well capable of scoring with most of the attacking coming down the flanks, Mayers on the overlap giving Scott Parker a new dimension to his Hammers offensive work.

Worryingly, Engels went over on his ankle just on the stroke of half time –  the teams went in at 0 – 0, a far more measured, controlled half than West Ham fans have been treated to in recent weeks.

#2077. Blackburn Rovers 2 – 1 West Ham United | Final whistle, first impressions as new manager bounce falls flat

West Ham managed to overturn their recent sequence of dreadful, lethargic starts with bright first half performance against Blackburn Rovers. Both sides had their chances but West Ham’s attack dominated the first half, largely through Austbø and Ezra Mayers down the left hand side.

The Hammers set up with Engels the deepest midfielder sitting in front of the back four and Kanté plus Mukasa the more forward of the trio. It seemed to protect the back line a little better as, apart from one looped shot over Hermansen’s goal, Blackburn’s threat was contained during the first 45 minutes.

Three or four times in the first ’45 Mayers overlapped after combining with Austbø – looking far more potent a threat than Solomon who he’d replaced – and got excellent crosses in from the left, an attacking option that had been lacking with Morato as the full back.

Piroe headed against the post early in the second half after Austbo – again – twisted and turned on the left, and Engles crashed the rebound just wide. Waves of pressure developed on the Blackburn goal as the Hammers responded to their half time talk but against the run of play from a break down the other end, Blackburn took the lead through Gudjohnson who headed through Hermansen’s legs. West Ham behind again.

Parker responded with Solomon for Austbø who’d run his socks off for an hour and Taty appearing in place of Kanté.

Controversy as Rovers scored a second with Kilman prostrate after a head collision – Dapo Afolayan the ex West Ham boy fired one into the corner leaving West Ham with a mountain to climb. It must be said, naive defending from West Ham.

Joel Piroe grabbed one back after a lucky bounce sat nicely for him in the box: 2 – 1 with eight minutes to go and the Ewood Park atmosphere changed, the home fans nervy and the Hammers fans in full voice. The minutes ticked away and West Ham struggled to get the ball towards Blackburn’s box: Orford, a late substitute, very fortunate to avoid conceding a penalty in the closing minutes – once again the lack of VAR coming to West Ham’s rescue.

Five minutes of added time, West Ham looking as if they had neither the urgency or the ability to surge forward again, fiddling about on the edge of their own box with Hermansen being booed every time he touched the ball. One last chance as Soucek headed straight at the ‘keeper in the last few seconds and that was that. Poor. Very poor. So much possession and so little to show for it.

#2076. Player Ratings: Blackburn 2-1 West Ham as Hermansen Has a Nightmare

West Ham’s promising start at Ewood Park ultimately counted for very little as Scott Parker’s side slipped to a 2-1 defeat against Blackburn Rovers. Despite enjoying plenty of possession and creating opportunities, the Hammers were undone by poor defending and some particularly questionable goalkeeping.

Joël Piroe’s late goal gave West Ham a chance of rescuing something, but the longer the game went on, the worse we seemed to play. There were some decent individual performances, particularly early on, but others will want to forget this afternoon in a hurry.

A really poor afternoon for the goalkeeper. I thought he could have been far more commanding for Blackburn’s opening goal, whether that meant catching the cross, punching it or simply getting something on the ball. He did make a straightforward late save from Todd Cantwell, but that doesn’t change my overall assessment.

One of West Ham’s more reliable performers before being substituted. Made some useful defensive interceptions and regularly pushed forward to support Bowen down the right. Tried a couple of long throws into the penalty area, although they didn’t really cause Blackburn much trouble.

Had some positive moments going forward, including a driving run from defence and a header that went narrowly wide early in the second half. However, I thought he could have done better for Blackburn’s first goal, and his performance deteriorated badly towards the end. Was fortunate not to concede a penalty before slipping twice during a dreadful passage of play that handed Blackburn a dangerous counter-attack.

Probably West Ham’s most dependable defender on the day. Made several important interceptions, particularly down the left where Blackburn repeatedly threatened, and was willing to carry the ball forward to help build attacks. Also produced a decent cross for Castellanos, although the resulting header went wide.

A mixed afternoon for the youngster. I was impressed with his willingness to get forward, his passing combinations with Austbø and some of the crosses he delivered. However, Blackburn repeatedly targeted his side, often leaving him facing two opponents, and he was beaten too easily in the build-up to the opening goal. Still very much learning the position.

Didn’t think he had a particularly good game. Had plenty of involvement, took the corners and got himself into shooting positions, but too often the final product was disappointing. Lost possession unnecessarily on occasions, failed to close down Blackburn’s second goalscorer quickly enough and wasted a promising late free kick with poor delivery.

You certainly couldn’t fault his work rate. At times he seemed to be everywhere, covering at left-back, appearing on the right and getting forward to support the attack. However, he wasn’t nearly as influential on the ball as he had been during the second half against Cardiff, and his shooting was disappointing. Replaced by Castellanos after 64 minutes.

One of West Ham’s more inventive players, particularly during the first half. Looked to move the ball quickly, attempted some clever through passes and wasn’t afraid to shoot, forcing one save and seeing another effort deflected behind. Not everything worked, but at least he was trying to make things happen.

I was genuinely surprised when he was substituted because he’d been one of West Ham’s livelier attacking players. Produced a lovely dribble past two defenders in the first half, linked up well with Mayers and delivered an excellent cross that Bowen headed against the post. Could perhaps have offered Mayers more defensive protection before Blackburn’s opener, but I thought he was contributing plenty going forward.

Blackburn 2-1 West Ham: Austbo was one of the Hammers better players

Worked hard to make things happen and was heavily involved in West Ham’s attacking play, particularly from the right. Unlucky to see his header strike the post following Austbø’s cross, while a difficult chance from close range went wide as he was falling and sliding. Also produced a lovely chipped delivery for Souček’s late header, but couldn’t quite provide the decisive contribution West Ham needed.

A frustrating performance rescued to some extent by an excellent goal. Too often he seemed hesitant in promising positions, allowing defenders to recover, while one particularly poor pass in the second half wasted a good attacking opportunity. However, he reacted brilliantly to Castellanos’ cross in the 82nd minute, firing high into the roof of the net. Whatever else you say about his performance, he took that chance extremely well.

Replaced Austbø after 58 minutes and was practically anonymous. Considering how involved Austbø had been, the substitution certainly didn’t improve West Ham’s attacking threat down the left.

Introduced for Kanté after 64 minutes and provided the cross that led to Piroe’s goal. Also had a header go wide from a Kilman delivery and was involved in the scramble that presented Bowen with a difficult chance. At least contributed something tangible to the attack.

Didn’t have a great deal of time to influence proceedings, particularly with West Ham having already lost their shape. Played one very silly ball into Orford inside our own penalty area, creating unnecessary danger. However, he also got into one of those familiar goalscoring positions in stoppage time, only to direct his header straight at the goalkeeper from Bowen’s excellent delivery.

Another substitute who came into a team that had lost its shape and was struggling for confidence. Was put in a difficult position by Souček’s poor pass inside the penalty area and was fortunate not to concede a penalty. Difficult to judge him too harshly given the limited time he had on the pitch and the state of the game when he entered.

#2075. Blackburn Rovers 2- 1 West Ham | Boos and ironic cheers highlight massive concern

THERE was an ironic cheer from the West Ham away supporters at about 88 minutes, which considering their team was 2- 1 down and looking clueless was even more remarkable.

The cheer was for Mads Hermansen finally making a save, with a shot hit straight at him being pretty much the first time he’d connected with anything, as another two goals had found their way under and past the hapless Dane.

7000 West Ham fans had made the trip to Blackburn in expectation of a triumphant start to Parker’s era and yet saw their starting eleven dominate the ball but fail to score. Hermansen had dealt with a smattering of booing from his own fans ever since Rovers took the lead with a header that went between the Dane’s legs.

Times’ up, Mads. The big concern was that Scott Parker picked him ahead of Areola. We told him….

Hardly a confidence boost for the young keeper who surely should not have been selected in the first place.

No criticism through could be attached to Hermansen for Blackburn’s second goal but West Ham found themselves two goals behind, chasing the game and seemingly nothing to offer, back passing and fiddling around in the last few minutes.

Parker can have no excuse now for continuing to select his hapless keeper. The Dane plays as if he’s got arthritic knees (take it fromm one who knows) and doesn’t dive for anything, just collapsing to the left or right, week after week.

Whatever issue there may be with second-in-line Alphonse Areola, he simply has to start after the international break.

Otherwise, we may as well simply drape a goal keeper’s jersey on the cross bar: It’ll be about as effective.

The most frustrating thing? We called this, as did just about every West Ham fan: Hermansen is just not good enough.

#2074. West Ham Go Full Circle as Blackburn Expose Familiar Problems

West Ham’s 2-1 defeat against Blackburn Rovers was a particularly frustrating result because, for large periods of the game, Scott Parker’s side appeared to be the better team. We started brightly, enjoyed plenty of possession and created opportunities, yet somehow managed to leave Ewood Park with nothing.

What concerns me most isn’t necessarily the result itself, although that’s bad enough. It’s the manner in which West Ham gradually deteriorated as the afternoon progressed. Even after Joël Piroe pulled a goal back late on, I thought we looked increasingly disorganised and short of confidence.

And that’s perhaps the strangest aspect of Parker’s first two matches. We started against Cardiff looking completely devoid of confidence, rediscovered it during that extraordinary second-half comeback, began confidently against Blackburn and somehow finished looking just as nervous as we had before.

I was actually quite encouraged by the opening stages. West Ham pressed high, moved the ball around reasonably well and looked determined to take the game to Blackburn. Max Kilman was particularly proactive, stepping out of defence to offer an additional passing option, while Divine Mukasa and Arne Engels were regularly involved in midfield.

Down the left, Ezra Mayers and Edvin Austbø developed a promising partnership. Mayers was willing to get forward and Austbø looked lively, producing one lovely piece of skill to beat two Blackburn players before delivering a dangerous cross.

Blackburn 2-1 West Ham: Austbo was one of the Hammers better players

However, there was a problem developing on that side of the pitch. Blackburn repeatedly managed to isolate Mayers against two opponents, and while the youngster was doing some good things offensively, he wasn’t receiving enough protection defensively.

Joël Piroe was also struggling to make the most of promising situations. On one occasion, he found himself with only a single defender to beat but hesitated for so long that three opponents eventually surrounded him. West Ham were having plenty of the ball, but Blackburn were defending deeply and making it difficult to create clear opportunities.

The second half initially offered more encouragement. Mavropanos headed narrowly wide from an Engels corner, Piroe had an effort saved and then Austbø produced an excellent cross which Bowen headed against the post. At that stage, West Ham were piling on the pressure and Blackburn were struggling to get out of their own half.

Then came the sucker punch. In the 54th minute, Blackburn broke down their right, with Mayers unable to stop the delivery into the penalty area. Andri Guðjohnsen converted, but I thought several West Ham players could have done better.

Austbø might have provided more protection for Mayers, Mavropanos could have defended the situation better and I certainly felt Mads Hermansen should have been more commanding. Whether he caught the cross, punched it or simply got something on the ball, I thought the goalkeeper had an opportunity to intervene.

It was a horrible goal to concede, particularly given how much of the attacking West Ham had been doing. Parker responded by introducing Manor Solomon for Austbø, a substitution I found surprising. The Norwegian had been one of our more involved attacking players, while Solomon subsequently struggled to make any impression.

Mohamadou Kanté was then replaced by Taty Castellanos, but West Ham were finding it increasingly difficult to establish the same attacking rhythm. Blackburn’s second goal arrived in the 71st minute, with Afolayan producing an excellent finish.

Kilman had gone down following contact to his face, but too many West Ham players appeared more interested in appealing for a foul than dealing with the danger. Engels, in particular, could have done more to close down the shot. Whatever the circumstances, you cannot simply stop defending because you believe the referee should have awarded a free kick.

At 2-0, the game appeared to be slipping away, but West Ham eventually found a route back through something remarkably straightforward. Castellanos got down the right-hand side and delivered a dangerous ball into the penalty area. Piroe reacted quickly and fired high into the roof of the net in the 82nd minute.

It was an excellent finish from a striker who, in truth, hadn’t been having a particularly good afternoon. But sometimes football really is that simple. Get the ball wide, get down the line and deliver something dangerous into the box. Give your centre-forward an opportunity to attack the ball.

Suddenly it was Blackburn 2-1 West Ham, with enough time remaining to rescue a point. Unfortunately, the expected late onslaught never really materialised. In fact, I thought West Ham became progressively worse.

Mavropanos endured a dreadful few minutes, fortunate not to concede a penalty before slipping and gifting Blackburn a counter-attack. He then slipped again while attempting to recover, while Souček subsequently played a very poor pass into Lewis Orford inside our own penalty area, creating another potentially disastrous situation.

West Ham looked increasingly nervous, and the defensive organisation seemed to disappear. There were still opportunities at both ends in stoppage time, with Todd Cantwell shooting straight at Hermansen when Blackburn might have made it 3-1.

Souček then headed directly at the Blackburn goalkeeper following an excellent chipped delivery from Bowen. It was precisely the sort of position from which we’ve seen Souček score numerous times, but once again West Ham had failed to make the most of a promising opportunity.

I keep coming back to the confidence issue because I think it explains an awful lot about what we’ve witnessed over these two matches. Against Cardiff, West Ham were absolutely dreadful during the opening 45 minutes, before producing a transformation after half-time that was almost impossible to believe.

Suddenly the players looked confident, aggressive and capable of playing some very good football. That improvement appeared to carry into the opening stages at Ewood Park, where we pressed Blackburn, moved the ball with purpose and looked considerably more comfortable in possession.

Yet by the closing stages, the confidence had completely evaporated. It was almost as though we’d gone full circle in the space of two matches, ending up precisely where we started. That is particularly disappointing because I still believe this West Ham squad possesses considerably more ability than recent performances suggest.

There were some positives. Mukasa showed invention, Austbø looked dangerous, Kilman had a decent game and Piroe took his goal extremely well. But the defensive mistakes, poor decision-making and increasingly nervous football were all too familiar.

I don’t think Scott Parker can be held responsible for everything we’ve witnessed this week. He’s barely had any meaningful time on the training pitch, and the international break offers him an opportunity to start properly implementing his ideas.

However, the evidence of these two games suggests that restoring confidence isn’t simply a matter of delivering one rousing team talk. The psychological side of West Ham’s problems may be every bit as important as the tactical side.

The frustrating thing is that we’ve already seen how much better these players can perform when they believe in themselves. Against Blackburn, we watched that belief gradually disappear again.

#2073. VAR a scourge on the Premier League as Forest denied by off-field meddling

Almost £3.5bn was splurged on transfers this summer in a league supposedly described as the best in the world, so why does VAR continue to prove so ineffective and divisive?

Seven years after its introduction, it remains a scourge on the Premier League and here at the City Ground was another exhibit of maddening off-field meddling.

Tottenham Hotspur avoided a third successive defeat after the crucial intervention of VAR prevented Neco Williams from securing Oliver Glasner his first win as Nottingham Forest’s head coach.

The big moment occurred in the 65th minute. Morgan Gibbs-White’s chip over Antonin Kinsky should have been dealt with by Sandro Tonali and Jan Paul van Hecke but both players got themselves in a muddle and Williams bundled the ball in from almost on the goal-line.

Replays appeared to show the ball went in off Williams’ knee and he was protecting his face with his hands to avoid a stray boot. The VAR review ruled that Williams had handled the ball, yet in this billion-pound industry there was not one camera angle which proved entirely conclusive.

On this occasion the VAR official was Peter Bankes, recommending to referee Craig Pawson that the goal be disallowed. Williams said: “It’s a goal. VAR is there when there is a clear and obvious error and for me that is not clear and obvious. I’ve seen the images and the replays and at not one moment did I think I handballed it because I never did. I headed it in between my arms. I’m at a loss at that one, it’s disappointing. If you’re going to pause it, it’s going to look like it hit my arm but it didn’t hit my arm.”

Glasner and the other Forest players were also incensed, and once again supporters are questioning how critical moments in matches are being decided by officials sitting at Stockley Park. “I think the VAR can’t intervene when he is guessing,” said Glasner. “I told the referee after the game that I felt the goal should have stood.

“The VAR should say to stay with the onfield decision because it is about strengthening the referee. If it’s not 100 per cent clear, stick to the onfield decision.  We had a briefing before the season that the threshold for VAR intervention this year should be very high which is why this is wrong.”

While Tottenham were perhaps fortunate to pick up their first point, they are still waiting to score their first Premier League goal of the season. They did not manage a shot on target.

The grand £350m rebuild is proving a slow-burner and it is only Mykhailo Mudryk who will have cause to remember such a dull affair. Signed on loan from Chelsea on deadline day, Mudryk made his first appearance since November 2024 after being suspended by the Football Association following a positive test for performance-enhancing meldonium.

The Ukrainian forward was introduced with 16 minutes left, with his manager Roberto De Zerbi determined to reinvigorate his career.

Tottenham are still waiting for lift-off but De Zerbi remains convinced that his team will eventually click, particularly in attacking areas.

One of their summer arrivals, Omar Marmoush, wasted their best chance in the 16th minute by drilling a shot wide of the post. De Zerbi said: “In the last third we have to improve. We have to maybe keep more calm when we are very close to doing something important.

“If we improve in the last third I think we can score many goals because we have the players with big qualities. We could have scored three or four goals.

Considering we were only all working together on Thursday for the first time, this is the right spirit and the right way to move on.” On Mudryk, De Zerbi said: “He’s working to reach the best physical condition and he needs time.”

After the disallowed Williams goal, Forest were feeling further aggrieved soon after when Rodrigo Bentancur appeared to pull back substitute Igor Jesus in the penalty area. These are two teams clearly in period of transition and patience will be required from both sets of supporters.

The big headline news from Tottenham is that Mykhailo Mudryk is on the bench.

Signed from Chelsea on deadline day on an initial loan, Mudryk was once branded as a future Ballon d’Or winner by Roberto De Zerbi after they worked together at Shakhtar.

Mudryk has not played a competitive match since November 2024 after being suspended by the Football Association following a positive test for performance-enhancing meldonium.

Enzo Fernández’s record deal to Manchester City was facilitated by English-founded agency Unique Sports Management, it can be revealed.

Fernández sealed a £125m move from Chelsea on deadline day, equalling the UK transfer record of Alexander Isak to Liverpool a year ago.

Football Association documents due to be published later in the season will show Unique to have played their part in the biggest transfer of the summer.

Fernández is represented by The Elegant Game, headed by ex-Argentina international Javier Pastore, although he is not registered with the FA for transfers in England.

Unique, which also represented Anthony Gordon for his move to Barcelona, were brought in to close the deal, which was agreed between clubs on deadline day afternoon.

The English-founded agency have Marc Guéhi, who moved to City in January, on their books and their summer deals included Gordon to Barca, Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea and Taylor Harwood-Bellis to Aston Villa. Troy Parrott, who scored the winner for Real Betis against Jose Mourinho’s Real Madrid, is also in the Unique stable.

Will this be third time lucky for Tottenham Hotspur after their £300m+ summer reset?

In typical Tottenham fashion, their start to the Premier League season has not been straightforward with two defeats, five goals conceded and none scored so far.

The popular opinion is that it will eventually click, but Tottenham’s supporters are still scarred by those two successive 17th-placed finishes.

Forest have won their last four games against Spurs, so it will be an early sign of promise if Roberto De Zerbi can secure a positive result here.

Enzo Maresca believes streetwise Enzo Fernández will give Manchester City an extra winning edge – as he told his record £125 million signing to forget about the size of the fee.

City made the Argentina midfielder the joint most expensive purchase in Premier League history with their deadline day swoop from Chelsea.

Maresca has opted against naming Fernández among his captains’ leadership group, which features Ruben Dias, Erling Haaland, Marc Guéhi and Gianluigi Donnarumma.

But the Italian – who knows Fernández well from their time together at Stamford Bridge – is confident his fierce competitive instincts will bring an added dimension to his side.

“I don’t know if it’s streetwise but he knows how to win,” Maresca said, who is in line to hand Fernández his debut against Coventry on Saturday. “When you want to compete or win, it’s much more important to have players that already know how to do that than players who have never done it in the past.

“Enzo is not the only one. This squad has many players who know how to win titles and how to compete and this is what we are looking for.

“I know Enzo quite well and I know what he can bring to the team. He is a winner, [has] a winner’s mentality and knows how to win [after] the World Cup, Club World Cup [success].

“I just said he is a winner and when you belong to the squad and another winning player arrives, they are always happy.

“I can promise you that in the last four or five days, four or five players from the squad were asking if was coming or not because they wanted him to be with us. It’s very important that he is with us.”

Maresca said he planned to use Fernandez predominantly as a No 6 or No 8 depending on the game. “I see Enzo as a six, a little bit more deep, or [an eight] a little higher arriving in the box,” he said.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Saturday afternoon 3pm kick-offs of which we are treated to a rare number this week as Sky and TNT Sports decide to inconvenience only 10 sets of matchgoing supporters rather than the usual 12 or 14. The matches start, purely alphabetically, with unbeaten Brentford hosting Sunderland, Leeds United travelling to Brighton and Hove Albion’s Amex Stadium where they have never won and have come away with only three points in their seven visits, the something’s-got-to-give quasi derby between winless Fulham and pointless Palace, leaders Man City hosting Coventry City for the Sky Blue Cup and Tottenham head to Nottingham Forest in pursuit of their first point to spoil the gaiety of a nation.

We have Mike McGrath reporting from the Etihad and John Percy at the City Ground and I will endeavour to keep you up to date with developments at the other three grounds via various methods. Forest vs Spurs seems the most consequential of the fixtures, not because either manager is in any danger but because now the window has closed it should give us a clearer picture of how Roberto De Zerbi plans to marshal his surfeit of wingers into a coherent attack that can break their goalscoring duck and how he proposes to organise a back four that have shipped five goals.

Fulham and Palace have come in for a lot of criticism regarding their recruitment and while I can understand the frustration of the former’s fans for doing so much business with Real Madrid, I think Gonzalo García is a proper player and will shine over the course of the season.

Palace, I think, are paying the price for the January splurge on Brennan Johnson and Jorgen Strand Larsen, not just the inflated fees but the sizeable wages on players who contributed almost nothing. I was at Leeds vs Brentford last week and there was plenty to admire about both sides but fear for Leeds’ so-far commendable resilience at their Amex knacker’s yard and wonder whether Sunderland will be able to live with Brentford’s pace. Manchester City vs Coventry, meanwhile, probably will not give us the Bouaddi-Fernández-Anderson £325m midfield from the start but we might be given a glimpse.

#2072. ‘Big call’ – Journalists react as Iraola names ‘exciting line-up’ for Liverpool in Istanbul

Andoni Iraola has made five changes to the Liverpool starting XI for tonight’s Champions League clash against Fenerbahce, with the head coach not afraid to drop some big names to the substitutes’ bench.

There’s a signficant reshuffle in attack as Florian Wirtz, Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak are all taken out of the line-up, with Dominik Szoboszlai, Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz coming in to start.

The Reds have no recognised centre-forward in their starting XI, so it looks likely that Bradley Barcola will move infield to lead the line.

When the team news was announced 75 minutes before kick-off, two Liverpool Echo reporters covering the game in Istanbul gave their immediate takes to some eye-catching selections by Iraola.

Paul Gorst wrote on the live matchday blog: ‘No recognised striker for Liverpool, so my hunch is it is Bradley Barcola who will lead the line tonight. It’s an exciting line-up, though. Munoz, Ngumoha, Szoboszlai all in there alongside Barcola.’

Ian Doyle focused on Trey Nyoni keeping his place alongside Alexis Mac Allister, saying: ‘Nyoni starts a third successive game, which is a big call. Not on form, but in terms of fitness for a youngster.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

A relentless fixture list and a quick turnaround from the defeat to Arsenal on Sunday has no doubt been a factor in Iraola making so many changes, but it’s by no means a weak starting XI for Liverpool.

The full-back combination of Joe Gomez and Kostas Tsimikas may seem surprising, but both are experienced campaigners who won’t wilt in the intense atmosphere of the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium.

The decision to persist with Nyoni is a tremendous show of faith in the teenager, whose recent performances suggest that he might’ve kept his place even if Ryan Gravenberch hadn’t been missing through injury.

The heavy rotation in the forward line is quite interesting, and at least Liverpool can point to having huge strength in depth off the bench is required. If it is Barcola who starts at centre-forward, a lot of eyes will be on him to see how he fares in that unfamiliar role.

Iraola hasn’t been afraid to roll the dice, which is an ideal trait for a head coach to have. He’s made some big calls tonight, and hopefully those will pay off and our 100% record in the Champions League will be preserved going into matchday five later this month.

#2071. Chickens come home to roost as the same pairing are exposed again.. and again.. West Ham News

West Ham United will have to make do without one of their – ahem – key players when the Championship resumes after the international break. Following on from today’s 2-1 defeat against a modest Blackburn Rovers side who knew exactly what they were about this afternoon, the Hammers go into a two week period of ‘deep reflection’ before restarting against Preston North End in two weeks time.

And they’ll have to do so without £4 million – oops that should read £40 million man Maximilian Kilman who picked up a fifth yellow card of the campaign – this one apparently for simulation after being smacked cleanly in the head –  and he will therefore sit out the first game back after the merciful lull in West Ham’s shambolic descent from the top end  of the table..

In depressing echoes of a year ago, West Ham still have to set up repeatedly with Kilman and Mavropanos as the defensive pairing of doom – only a matter of time before one, or other of them is caught hopelessly out of position.

At least Dinos Mavropanos offers a goal threat – whilst when paired with Kilman is made to look defensively distinctly ordinary

In what can only be seen as a massive mistake, West Ham chose not to add to their centre back keystone cops double act in the summer window, letting Todibo leave on loan and therefore both committing and condemning themselves to the duo for the foreseeable future.

West Ham solved the problem last year – but not the number of points lost – by bringing in Axel Disasi in the January window and you’d expect them to make a similar move for an urgent upgrade this winter. Too little, too late, much as it was a year ago.

We can only hope that Airidas Golambeckis impresses enough in his outing alongside Dinos in two weeks’ time that he keeps Kilman out of the side.

To be honest, it is tough watching the same pairing year after year making the same mistakes and costing clean sheet after clean sheet. Having a goalkeeper with the arms of a five year old doesn’t help but until West Ham wake up, smell the coffee and realise that Mavropanos and Kilman will never be more than mediocre, the same results will flow, week in, week out.

#2070. Glasgow biotech teams up with Nottingham Forest to trial injury risk blood test

A Glasgow biotech company has teamed up with Premier League club Nottingham Forest to investigate whether blood tests could help identify injury risks in professional footballers before they happen.

Entourage, based at Kelvin Campus, is conducting a 12-week study involving the club’s 25-player men’s B team, with support from Scottish Enterprise.

The Entourage Team. (Image: Martin Shields)

The research will use plasma proteomics, the analysis of proteins in blood, to monitor players’ biological responses to training, matches and recovery.

Players will provide blood samples twice a week, allowing researchers to analyse thousands of proteins and track individual responses to physical demands, injuries and recovery.

By combining the results with existing training, workload and clinical information, the team hopes to identify protein patterns that could indicate a greater risk of non-contact soft tissue injuries.

The trial is described as the first high-frequency plasma proteomic study involving a professional sports team.

A blood sample being collected. (Image: Supplied)

The research comes amid concerns about the impact of hamstring injuries in elite football. UEFA figures for the 2021/22 season found they accounted for one in five days of injury absence across elite European football, double the rate recorded two decades earlier.

Entourage’s technology focuses on using protein analysis to better understand inflammation, immune function and recovery. The company is also building a reference dataset for elite athletes, supported by its research centre at Kelvin Campus.

The findings could help clubs develop more personalised training and recovery plans based on players’ individual biological responses.

The company also sees potential applications for its technology beyond sport, including the early detection of conditions such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes and Alzheimer’s.

Entourage lab technician Matthew Mitchell prepares a blood sample for testing in their lab. (Image: Elaine Livingstone)

Entourage was co-founded by Professor Patrick Gunning, Dr Taleb Sedghi and Dr Mark Lindsay and launched with a $5 million pre-seed funding round.

Professor Gunning previously co-founded Dunad Therapeutics and helped secure a $1.3 billion partnership with Novartis.

The company plans to report its findings to Nottingham Forest at the end of the 12-week study.

Voluntary Health Scotland relaunches as Health Creation Scotland to tackle inequality

Century-old foundation stone restored and relocated at Aberdeen children's hospital

Aberdeen 'set' to sack Stephen Robinson as axe looms at Pittodrie

Professor Patrick Gunning, chief executive and co-founder of Entourage, said:"One of the questions we are trying to answer is whether there are signals in the blood that could indicate an increased risk of a non-contact injury.

"That is something we need to investigate through the study."

Dimitrios Kalogiannidis, head of medical at Nottingham Forest, said: "We are deeply committed to evidence-led player care.

"We believe in the importance of building a more robust biological profile of each player, so we’re pleased to be taking part in this research study that could benefit Nottingham Forest and the wider game for years to come."

Entourage’s chief executive and co-founder, Professor Patrick Gunning pictured with lab scientist Daniel Poloske. (Image: Elaine Livingstone)

Dr Mark Lindsay, co-founder of Entourage, said: "We're moving soft-tissue care from estimation to measurement.

"We read the biology of the injury, precision directives guide every stage of treatment, and return to play is decided by the data.

"You can't manage what you can't measure."

#2069. Blackburn Rovers 2- 1 West Ham United | The morning after

Scott Parker’s words at full time pretty much summed up the remainder of this Championship season for West Ham United following the side’s first away defeat of the campaign. The new manager bounce failed to materialise as his squad thew away chance after chance against their solid opponents who twice capitalised on the now-traditional lacklustre Irons’ defending.

Speaking after the game to BBC Radio London, a hoarse Hammers head coach declared :

Not only at Ewood Park, but in the 31 remaining games of this season. A six point gap between the Hammers in ninth and the league leaders is not yet insurmountable. But it is, certainly, a mountain to climb for Parker to turn West Ham’s dreadfully mediocre-looking squad into Championship contenders.

With so many leaks, it is difficult to know which hole to plug first in the slowly sinking good ship West Ham United. Goalkeeper, defence, midfield, attack – all are areas crying out for urgent post-Nuno repair.. But none are yet beyond salvage.

A tough watch – Scott Parker will have learned a lot about his West Ham squad

As many have commented, though, it’s going to be a long season.

Right now, half a season of the dour, drab, boring but solid wins for which Scott Parker received so much criticism from his time at Burnley would be pretty well received in east London.

Usually we curse the international break but I have a feeling this time around it comes as a huge relief to the manager, the squad and supporters, for very different reasons. Amongst supporters, optimism will no doubt resurface at some stage during the next fortnight as we convince ourselves that if nothing else, we have the right man for the job at the helm.

Whatever Scott Parker is getting paid, if he somehow manages to transform this group into his trademark mean, lean, tough side capable of grinding out one-nil victories week in, week out, frankly he’ll be worth every penny.

#2068. “Erased” – Media explanation for one star’s waning at West Ham United

West Ham’s Nuno- divided squad was rallied midweek by new manager Scott Parker with his declaration that the slate had been wiped clean and that everyone had a chance to impress. However, anxious voices across the Atlantic continue to berate West Ham for ruining the career of Mexico’s national team captain Edson Alvarez.

Few in Central America seem able to understand el Machin’s fall from grace, despite both injury and scandal dogging the midfielder during the summer. Edson Alvarez pictured back in training in Parker’s pre-Blackburn session.

“91 days in oblivion, with Alvarez still erased from West Ham.

Whereas the first two sides picked may well have been a ‘committee’ selection involving his coaching team, since the new manager only rocked up on Wednesday, two weeks with virtually his whole squad including the likes of Magassa and Alvarez will allow Parker to judge for himself who has the cojones to give his West Ham line up some much-needed moral fibre.

West Ham settled on Austbø – and appear to have done pretty well by signing the up and coming young winger

Before joining Middlesbrough, Cozier-Duberry enjoyed an outstanding loan spell with Bolton Wanderers in League One last season. He scored 11 goals and contributed 13 assists, underlining his reputation as one of the country’s most promising young attacking talents.

At West Ham, Manor Solomon has experienced a mixed start to his spell in east London, while Austbø has already chipped in with two goals and two assists despite largely being used as a substitute.

#2066. West Ham fans’ furious reaction raises an uncomfortable question

As the Hammers subsided to their first away defeat in the Championship, long suffering supporters, who’d undertaken the 480 mile round trip to be served up a pretty spineless team performance, decided to let their team have it with both barrels.

After last week’s displeasure culminating an Hammers fans singing ‘sacked in the morning’ to their own manager, this weekend brought the players into the crosshairs as the next logical target for their ire.

..With Nuno Espirito Santo out of the job and with Scott Parker just 72 hours in, the 7,500+ travelling fans turned on their stars.

Under no illusions after the result – and the away fans’ response – yesterday: Scott Parker

..As well as booing their own goal keeper pretty much throughout, if the reports on the radio were correct.

Traditionalists will likely be aghast at the thought of fans undermining their own team in this manner, whilst those who participated no doubt feel it was the only way to show their contempt for the perceived lack of commitment and effort which those eleven representatives  of the Claret and Blue heritage displayed.

Not to mention the hundreds of pounds it costs each supporter, every game, merely to arrive at the turnstiles in support of our club. But is it the ‘right’ thing to do?

For me – it’s a no. I started attending games with my son when he was ten years old and however bad it got (it was pretty dire in that season of 2003-4) we never left early, never booed our own players (Luis Boa Morte excepted, I must confess to once letting my frustration with his indolence bubble over) and always, always applauded those who’d put in a shift, regardless of outcome. And I’d not even heard ‘you’re not fit to wear the shirt‘ sung by West Ham fans in my couple of decades’ worth of attending games.

I just don’t see it helping team morale or positively influencing the final outcome. Which is, after all, the point of ‘supporters’.

Giving ‘The Sun’ another gleeful headline to point out our sufferings sticks in my throat too.

But don’t get me wrong, each has absolutely the right to their own response. Just don’t see it helping is all.
